paras: The killing of Bonaparte Smith took place at the polls in Milton, Kentucky, on election day, August 2, 1880, when Smith, a Black man, was knocked down and fatally stabbed and beaten. The man who did the stabbing, whose name the papers printed as Coruman, Cornham or Cornman, was arrested. Northern and Western papers carried the news as an "election stabbing" and an "election riot", and one headed it "Nothing Like a Free Ballot."

According to a special dispatch from Madison, Indiana, to the Gazette, dated August 2, Smith was knocked down at the polls at Milton that day and then "fatally stabbed and beaten." Weekly digests later described the attack as an "election riot" on the 2d. No report says how the trouble at the polls began, who else took part, or what the assailant's race was.

The man identified as the stabber was arrested, according to the first dispatch and the later digests. No report of an inquest, indictment or trial appears in the coverage, and no Kentucky paper's account was found.

Only white papers outside Kentucky carried the story, almost all of them in the words of the Madison special. On August 3 the St. Paul Daily Globe printed it under "ELECTION STABBING.", while the Rock Island Argus ran it in a column of crimes. The Sacramento Daily Record-Union gave the same text the ironic headline "Nothing Like a Free Ballot." The Press and Daily Dakotaian ran it twice on August 4 under "LATEST BY MAIL.", and the Worthington Advance repeated the Globe's version on August 5.

A week later, Minnesota and Wisconsin weeklies folded the case into crime digests titled "Recent Tragedies." and "THE CRIMINAL CALENDAR.", calling it an "election riot". The Daily Republican did not name Smith but counted the Milton riot among the murders reported across several states that Monday. No Black newspaper coverage of the killing was found.

The accused's name appears as "Coruman" in the first dispatch, "Cornham" in two digests and "Cornman" in the Mankato Free Press, probably variants of one name. The Daily Republican alone said that a sixth man was "dangerously, it not fatally wounded" in the riot, without naming him or giving his race.

framing.detail: The Daily Globe ran the special under 'ELECTION STABBING.' without comment.
The Sacramento Daily Record-Union headed the same special 'Nothing Like a Free Ballot.', an ironic comment on violence at a Southern poll.
Minnesota and Wisconsin weeklies folded it into 'Recent Tragedies.' and 'THE CRIMINAL CALENDAR.' digests as an 'election riot'.
The Daily Republican counted it among a day's murders across several states, without naming Smith.
